problem: A particle $P$ is moving along the curve $y={x}^{2}-6x$ such that the $x$-coordinate of $P$ is changing at the rate of $3\,\text{cm}/\text{s}.$ Find the rate of change of the $y$-coordinate when $x=2\,\text{cm}.$

examples.knowledge_point: Determining the Rate of Change of an XY-Coordinate
examples.problem: A particle $P$ is moving along the curve $y=x+e^x$ such that the $x$-coordinate of $P$ is changing at the rate of $2 \,\textrm{cm}/\textrm{s}.$ Find the rate of change of the $y$-coordinate when $x=5\,\textrm{cm}.$
examples.worked_solution:
Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =x+{e}^{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(x+{e}^{x}) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x+{e}^{x}) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot (1+{e}^{x}).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can substitute the given information $\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}=2 \,\textrm{cm}/\textrm{s}$ and $x=5$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =2(1+{e}^{5})\,\text{cm}/\text{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem: Given that $r=\theta +6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ for $\theta =\theta (t),$ and that $\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}=7$ at the point where $\theta =\frac{7\pi }{6},$ find $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\theta +6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(r) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\theta +6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\theta +6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}\cdot (1-6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Now we can substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}=7$ and $\theta =\frac{7\pi }{6},$ and solve for $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}\cdot (1-6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =7\cdot (1-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{6})) \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =7\cdot 4 \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =28.\end{aligned}
$$
